newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends on upbeat note in U.S. before jobs, G7.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends on upbeat note in U.S. before jobs, G7.

text.p: *Dollar closed higher against most major currencies amid hope G7 will not talk dollar down this weekend and specualtion that German rates could head lower. German unemployment surged to 4.66 million in Jan. Jobless rate 12.2 pct Jan vs 10.8 pct Dec.
*U.S. jobs data due Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Jan payrolls
seen +237,000. Jan jobless rate seen 5.2 pct vs Dec 5.3 pct.

The dollar ended barely higher versus the yen and mark amid hope that financial leaders meeting this weekend will not try to talk the dollar down and belief that German interest rates may soon fall, experts said.
Volume in the currency market, however, was subdued as traders awaited the meeting as well as a key report on the U.S. jobs market due out on Friday.
Key financial leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) major industrial powers will convene in Berlin on Saturday.
"It's been a very quiet day, very little activity," said John McCarthy, a senior vice president at ING Capital Markets.

"I don't think the G7 is going to say anything too dramatic one way or the other," McCarthy added. "Some thoughts are given to the fact that they may say something about the pace of the dollar's rise."
The dollar hit 124 yen for the first time in four years on Thursday and also climbed to 1.6548 marks but then retreated.
The dollar closed at 123.70/80 yen and 1.6530/40 marks, up from 123.66/71 yen and 1.6520/30 marks at the open.
The dollar had plunged to post World War II lows of 1.3438 marks on March 8, 1995 and 79.75 yen on April 19 of that year. Since then, the U.S. unit has rallied sharply.
On Thursday, the German Finance Ministry characterized recent moves in the currency markets as a "normalization" from conditions prevailing in early 1995.
The Ministry said it expects the weekend talks to conclude that current conditions are favorable for continued German economic growth due to low interest rates and exchange rates.
Also, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt and French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis endorsed recent currency moves.
Taken together, the remarks seemed to indicate financial leaders this weekend may not try to talk the dollar down but instead will emphasize the need for stable currency rates.

"That's really what's in place here, is that the markets don't anticipate any central bank intervention to stem the dollar's rise," said Talbott Young, a vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank.

U.S. jobs data due out Friday was preceded by German jobs figures on Thursday that helped boost the dollar against the mark. German unemployment surged by more than half a million to a new post war record of 4.66 million in January, a level last seen in the depths of the Great Depression of the 1930s.
The jobless rate jumped to 12.2 percent in January from 10.8 percent in December.
The weak economic data "suggest that a rate hike is a long way off and an ease is possible," said Kevin Harris, an international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch.
Harris also noted that market interest rates could remain lower amid sluggish economic conditions.
"Demand for marks on an investment basis is going to soften if it looks like domestic investment in Germany won't carry as high a return," Harris added.
Widely watched U.S. employment numbers are set to be released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Friday.

Economists polled by Reuters, on average, predicted non-farm payrolls increased 237,000 in January after gaining 262,000 in December. The jobless rates is seen edging lower to 5.2 percent from 5.3 percent.
Elsewhere, the dollar finished at 1.4263/73 Swiss francs, up from 1.4255/65 francs at the open. Sterling fell to $1.6330/40 from $1.6399/04.
The dollar ended at Canadian $1.3501/06, up from C$1.3468/73. The Australian dollar finished at $0.7643/48, down from $0.7645/50 at the open.
